questions.question: What do the three fields in `Request(prefix_tokens, suffix_tokens, prefix_key)` represent in the simulator?
options: Reusable prefix tokens, suffix tokens, and a prefix key
The model's output length, cache TTL, and the provider's API key
Three alternative prices for one request, selected by the provider at runtime
The number of writes, reads, and misses that have already occurred
questions.explanation: The simulator treats `prefix_tokens` as cacheable, `suffix_tokens` as the changing user portion, and `prefix_key` as the equality key used by each provider's cache map.

questions.question: In `simulate_anthropic`, when is an existing prefix considered expired?
options: When the current request has a different suffix, even if the prefix key is unchanged
When elapsed time reaches the entry's TTL, causing a new write
Only after exactly two reads, because the simulator caps cache reuse at two requests
When the prefix contains fewer than 1,024 tokens, regardless of elapsed time
questions.explanation: The expiry condition is `entry is None or (now_seconds - entry.written_at) >= entry.ttl_seconds`. A miss writes the prefix at the current simulated time; an unexpired entry is a read.

questions.question: What TTL does `simulate_openai` use for its automatic cache model?
options: Five minutes, matching Anthropic's short-lived cache
The caller's `ttl_seconds` argument, which OpenAI receives explicitly
A fixed 3,600-second best-effort window in this simulator
No TTL; every matching prefix remains cached for the entire process
questions.explanation: Unlike the Anthropic and Gemini helpers, `simulate_openai` takes only the requests and interval. Its expiry test uses the hard-coded `3600` seconds.

questions.question: What pattern of prefix keys does `make_traffic(n_requests=6, n_prefixes=3, ...)` produce?
options: Six unique keys, because every request receives a fresh prefix identifier
Only `prefix_0`, because the first prefix is reused for all traffic
Keys chosen randomly from three strings, so counts vary on every run
`prefix_0`, `prefix_1`, `prefix_2`, then the same three keys repeated
questions.explanation: The list comprehension uses `prefix_key=f"prefix_{i % n_prefixes}"`. With six requests and three prefixes, each rotating key occurs twice.

questions.question: What does `baseline_cost(requests, provider)` deliberately ignore?
options: It prices every prefix and suffix token at the provider's base input rate
The suffix token count, because only the reusable prefix can affect cost
The selected provider, because all entries in `PRICES` use the same base rate
The number of requests, because baseline is calculated from a single representative entry
questions.explanation: The baseline sums `(prefix_tokens + suffix_tokens) / 1000 * p["base"]` for every request. It is the no-cache comparison point against which provider cache savings are reported.

questions.question: Why does `simulate_gemini` add a `storage_cost` after processing requests?
options: Gemini charges storage for each generated suffix token even when no prefix is cached
It charges retained prefixes by token-hours over their TTL
Storage cost is a proxy for output-token generation and is added only when reads outnumber writes
The simulator uses storage cost to replace input cost whenever the cache has a miss
questions.explanation: After the request loop, each retained cache entry contributes `tokens/1000 * storage_per_1k_per_hour * ttl_seconds/3600`. This models Gemini's separate token-hour storage charge.
